trials.notes: Functional result: 11/11. Correctly chose WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment(), used a bookmark on the list opener, bounded the subtree scan with next_token() and get_current_depth(), counted only non-closing LI tag tokens at direct-child depth, rejected incomplete or unsupported scans, sought back, set the attribute, and returned get_updated_html(). All API calls are documented in the two rendered files.

Functional result: 11/11. Same core pattern as trial 1: HTML Processor, bookmark/seek, token walk, get_token_type() check, direct-child depth check, incomplete and unsupported guards, set_attribute(), and get_updated_html(). The class_exists() guard is unnecessary but not an HTML API hallucination.

Functional result: 9/11. Correct processor and documented methods, with proper bookmark/seek/get_updated_html usage. The main adherence problem is the subtree scan: it uses plain next_tag(), whose default skips closers, then expects a depth drop to mark the end of the list. Because the list closer is skipped, the scan continues past the first list and treats later incomplete or unsupported markup as if the list scan failed. It can also overcount LI elements inside later sibling containers.

failure_analysis: Trials 1 and 2 passed every hidden case, largely because the rendered docs supplied the right high-level recipe: use WP_HTML_Processor for structure, record the opener depth, walk tokens while depth remains within the subtree, check get_token_type(), use bookmarks to return to the opener, then call get_updated_html(). Trial 3 failed incomplete-token-after-closed-list and unsupported-after-closed-list. The misconception was that a plain next_tag() loop plus get_current_depth() < $list_depth would stop at the end of the first list. The docs for HTML Processor next_tag() say tag_closers defaults to skip, and the get_current_depth() section explains that the depth drop occurs at the element's own closing token. However, those two facts are not tied together strongly enough: if closers are skipped, that boundary token is never observed. The candidate therefore scanned beyond the closed list; paused_at_incomplete_token() or get_last_error() came from later markup, not from an incomplete first-list scan. The same misunderstanding would also affect non-hidden cases with a later sibling container containing LI elements, because the candidate can count those later LI openers as if they were direct children of the first list.

doc_gaps.problem: The depth-boundary rule says the first token below the opener depth is the element's own closer, but it does not explicitly say this only works if the walk actually visits closing tokens.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a warning and short example: use next_token(), or next_tag( array( 'tag_closers' => 'visit' ) ), for depth-bounded subtree walks. Plain next_tag() skips closers and can continue past the container into later document content.

doc_gaps.problem: The default tag_closers => skip behavior is documented, but the practical consequence for subtree scans is easy to miss.
doc_gaps.suggestion: After the tag_closers parameter description, add a structural-scan note: code that must detect when an element closes must opt into closers or use next_token(); otherwise depth checks cannot see the container boundary.

doc_gaps.location: Recipe: scan a region before editing its opener
doc_gaps.problem: The recipe uses next_token() correctly, but it does not contrast that with the tempting but wrong plain next_tag() variant.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Extend the recipe with a brief 'do not use plain next_tag() for this boundary check' note, explaining that later parse errors after the region should not invalidate a completed region-local mutation.

doc_gaps.location: Recipe: test subtree membership and direct children
doc_gaps.problem: The direct-child predicate is shown, but the full loop boundary is not reinforced at the same point.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Include a compact direct-child-count loop that records container depth, walks with next_token() or next_tag(... tag_closers visit), breaks only when depth drops below the container depth, and then applies the direct-child opener predicate.
